title: That men by various ways arrive at the same end
paragraphs: The usual way to soften the anger of someone we have offended, when they hold the power of revenge and we lie entirely at their mercy, is to submit — to move them to pity and compassion. And yet bravery, constancy, and resolution, the opposite means, have sometimes produced the same effect.

Edward, Prince of Wales — the Black Prince, who long governed our Guienne, a man whose fortune and character carried much of the most striking grandeur — had been provoked beyond bearing by the Limousins. When he took their city by assault, no cries from the people, no prayers and tears of women and children flung at his feet, could stop his revenge. It was only further inside the town, when he came across three French gentlemen who alone, with unbelievable courage, were still holding off his victorious army, that consideration and respect for such valour first checked the torrent of his fury. His clemency began with these three knights, and from them spread to all the remaining inhabitants of the city.

Scanderbeg, Prince of Epirus, was chasing one of his own soldiers with intent to kill him. The soldier, having tried every form of humility and supplication in vain, resolved as a last resort to turn, plant himself, and wait sword in hand. The sudden steadiness brought his captain's fury to a stop, and seeing the man take so striking a stance, Scanderbeg pardoned him. The story could of course be read otherwise by anyone unfamiliar with that prince's prodigious courage and might.

The Emperor Conrad III, besieging Guelph, Duke of Bavaria, would accept no mean or unmanly satisfaction whatever as a condition for mercy, and would settle for nothing softer than this: that the ladies and gentlewomen with the duke in the town might walk out, unharmed in honour, on foot, carrying only what they could lift themselves. Whereupon they, magnanimous, hoisted their husbands and children — and the duke himself — onto their shoulders and carried them out. The emperor, ravished by the generosity of it, wept for joy, and the deadly hatred he had carried against the duke vanished on the spot; from that day on he treated the duke and his with full humanity. Either of those two methods would work easily on me, for I have an unusual leaning toward mercy and mildness — so much so that I think I would surrender my anger sooner to compassion than to admiration. Pity, of course, is reckoned a vice among the Stoics, who require that we help the afflicted but not be so affected as to suffer with them. I thought these examples not ill suited to the question at hand, all the more because in them we see great souls assaulted and tested by two very different means: resisting one without yielding, and being shaken and subdued by the other. It may be true that letting one's heart be wholly conquered by compassion can be put down to weakness, softness, and over-tenderness — which is why the weaker natures, women, children, and the common sort, are the most susceptible to it. But to have resisted and scorned the power of groans and tears, and then to yield only to the bare reverence of the sacred image of Valour — this can only be the work of a strong and inflexible soul in love with and honouring masculine, obstinate courage. Even so, astonishment and admiration may produce a similar effect in less generous minds. Witness the people of Thebes, who put two of their generals on trial for their lives for having kept arms past the precise term of their commission. They only just pardoned Pelopidas, who bowed under the weight of so dangerous a charge and offered no defence but prayers and supplications; while Epaminondas, by contrast, launched grandly into a recital of the great deeds he had done in their service, and reproached them haughtily and arrogantly for ingratitude and injustice — and they had not the heart to push the trial further, broke up the court, and went home, the assembly loudly praising the man's high courage.

Dionysius the Elder, after a long siege and great difficulty, took the city of Reggio and with it the governor Phyton, a very gallant man whose defence had been unyielding. Dionysius decided to make a tragic example of his revenge. He began by telling Phyton that he had, the day before, ordered his son and all his relatives drowned. Phyton's only reply was that they were by one day happier than he was. Dionysius then had him stripped and handed to the tormentors, who dragged him through the streets of the town and most cruelly whipped him, all the while heaping bitter insults on him. He kept his courage intact the whole way, voice strong and face undaunted, declaring out loud the honourable and glorious cause of his death: that he would not surrender his country into the hands of a tyrant. And he called down on Dionysius a swift punishment from the offended gods. Reading in his soldiers' faces that, far from being offended by the prisoner's haughty speech to the contempt of their captain and his triumph, they were struck with admiration for so rare a virtue and inclined to mutiny — even ready to rescue the prisoner from the executioner — Dionysius stopped the torture and, in private, had Phyton thrown into the sea.

Man, in truth, is a marvellously vain, fickle, and unstable subject, and one on whom it is very hard to form any certain and uniform judgment. Pompey could pardon the whole city of the Mamertines, though furiously incensed at it, solely on the strength of the virtue and magnanimity of a single citizen, Zeno, who took the city's fault entirely on himself and asked no other favour than to be punished alone for all. And yet Sylla's host, who in the city of Perugia showed the same virtue, got nothing by it, either for himself or for his fellow citizens.

And, directly contrary to my first examples, the bravest of all men, the one most famous for clemency to those he overcame — Alexander — after great difficulty stormed the city of Gaza. Entering, he found Betis, its commander, of whose valour during the siege he had had striking and repeated proof, standing alone, abandoned by his soldiers, his armour hacked to pieces, drenched in blood and wounds, and still fighting in a crowd of Macedonians striking him from every side. Alexander, nettled at so dear-bought a victory — he had two fresh wounds of his own — said to him: 'You shall not die as you intend, Betis. You shall suffer every torment that can be inflicted on a captive.' To which Betis answered only with a fierce and disdainful look. 'What,' said Alexander, watching his haughty, obstinate silence, 'is he too stiff to bend a knee? Too proud to utter one suppliant word? Then I will conquer this silence. If I cannot force a word from his mouth, I will at least extract a groan from his heart.' And turning his anger into fury, he ordered Betis's heels bored through and had him dragged alive, mangled and torn apart, at the back of a cart. Was it that the height of courage was so natural and familiar to this conqueror that, since he could not admire it, he respected it less? Or that he held valour to be so peculiarly his own that his pride could not, without envy, endure it in another? Or that the natural impetuosity of his fury was simply incapable of opposition? Surely, had it been capable of moderation, the sack and ruin of Thebes would have moderated it: to see so many valiant men, lost and without further defence, slaughtered before his eyes — above six thousand put to the sword, of whom not one was seen to flee or heard to cry for quarter, but every one running here and there to seek out the victorious enemy and provoke them to give him an honourable end. Not one was seen who, however weakened by wounds, did not in his last gasp still try to take revenge, and with all the weapons of a brave despair to sweeten his own death in the death of an enemy. Yet their valour drew no pity, and the length of one day was not enough to satisfy the conqueror's thirst for revenge. The slaughter went on to the last drop of blood that could be shed, and stopped only when it met none but unarmed people — old men, women, and children — thirty thousand of whom were carried away as slaves.

title: Of sorrow
paragraphs: No man living is more free of this passion than I am, and I neither indulge it in myself nor admire it in others, even though the world has settled on giving it a particular esteem — dressing wisdom, virtue, and conscience in its colours. A foolish and squalid disguise. The Italians more aptly call this temperament malignity, for it is always hurtful, always idle and vain, and being cowardly, mean, and base, it is by the Stoics expressly forbidden to their sages.

The story goes that Psammenitus, King of Egypt, was defeated and taken prisoner by Cambyses, King of Persia. When his own daughter passed by him as a prisoner, in a wretched dress, carrying a bucket to draw water, his friends around him broke down in tears and lamentation; he himself stayed unmoved, said nothing, and kept his eyes on the ground. He kept the same face when, moments later, he saw his son led to execution. But when at last he spotted one of his own household friends being dragged off among the captives, he tore at his hair and beat his breast with all the extravagance of extreme grief.

A story that pairs well with another of recent date about a prince of our own nation, who at Trent received word of the death of his elder brother — the man on whom the whole standing and honour of his house depended — and shortly after of the death of a younger brother, the family's second hope. He bore both blows with exemplary resolution. A few days later, when one of his servants happened to die, his constancy gave way; he abandoned himself to grief and mourning, leading some to conclude that it was only this last stroke of fortune that had really wounded him. The truth was that, being already brimful of grief, the smallest addition overflowed the bounds of all patience. I think the same might be said of the earlier example, were it not that the story tells us Cambyses asked Psammenitus why, if he was not moved by the calamity of his son and daughter, he should so impatiently bear the misfortune of his friend. 'Because,' he answered, 'this last grief is small enough to be shown by tears; the other two go beyond any expression at all.'

Something like this may have been working in the imagination of the ancient painter who, in painting the sacrifice of Iphigenia, had to show the sorrow of those standing by in proportion to the interest each had in the death of this beautiful innocent girl. Having spent the full power of his art on the other figures, when he came to her father he painted him with a veil over his face, meaning that no expression of feature was equal to the grief he had to show. It is the same reason the poets pretend that the miserable mother, Niobe, after losing seven sons and then as many daughters and being overwhelmed by her losses, was at last turned into a rock —
"Diriguisse malis,"
["Petrified with her misfortunes." — Ovid, Met., vi. 304.]

— meaning to express that melancholy, dumb, and deaf stupefaction which numbs all our faculties when we are overwhelmed by something larger than we can carry. The violence of an excessive grief does of necessity astonish the soul and rob her of her ordinary functions, as happens to any of us, when on hearing some sudden bad news we find ourselves surprised, stupefied, and almost incapable of motion — until the soul, beginning to let itself out in tears and lamentation, seems to free and disengage itself from the first oppression, and find some room to work itself out more freely.
"Et via vix tandem voci laxata dolore est."
["And at length, with difficulty, grief opens a passage for the voice." — Aeneid, xi. 151.]

In Ferdinand's war against the widow of King John of Hungary, around Buda, a man-at-arms drew everyone's notice for his singular gallantry in a particular encounter; he was widely praised and mourned when he was left dead on the field — and by no one more than Raisciac, a German lord who had been deeply taken with so rare a valour. When the body was brought off and the count, out of common curiosity, came to look at it, the armour was no sooner removed than he recognised his own son — a thing that added a second blow to the compassion of all the bystanders. Without saying a word, without taking his eyes from the wretched object, he stood fixedly contemplating the body of his son, until the violence of his sorrow overcame his vital spirits and dropped him stone-dead to the ground.
"Chi puo dir com' egli arde, a in picciol fuoco,"
["He who can say how he burns with love has only a small fire." — Petrarca, Sonetto 137.]
— say the Innamorati, when they want to render an unbearable passion.

"Misero quod omneis Eripit sensus mihi: nam simul te, Lesbia, aspexi, nihil est super mi, Quod loquar amens. Lingua sed torpet: tenuis sub artus Flamma dimanat; sonitu suopte Tintinant aures; gemina teguntur Lumina nocte."

["Love takes all my faculties from me: Lesbia, the moment I'm in your presence I cannot say a word for my distracted passion; my tongue is numb; a thin flame creeps under my limbs; my ears ring with their own noise; my eyes are veiled in double darkness." — Catullus, Epig. li. 5.]

Nor is it in the height and full fury of the fit that we are in any condition to pour out complaints or amorous persuasions; the soul is overburdened then, labouring with deep thoughts, and the body sunk in languid desire. From which sometimes come those accidental impotencies that so unseasonably surprise the lover, and that frigidity which, by the force of an immoderate ardour, seizes him even in the lap of fulfilment. For every passion that lets itself be tasted and digested is, by that very fact, moderate:
"Curae leves loquuntur, ingentes stupent."
["Light griefs can speak; deep sorrows are dumb." — Seneca, Hippolytus, act ii. scene 3.]
A surprise of unexpected joy often produces the same effect:
"Ut me conspexit venientem, et Troja circum Arma amens vidit, magnis exterrita monstris, Diriguit visu in medio, calor ossa reliquit, Labitur, et longo vix tandem tempore fatur."

["When she saw me coming and, terrified, recognised the Trojan armour around me, she stood frozen at the sight; the warmth left her bones; she sinks down, and only after a long interval can she at last speak." — Aeneid, iii. 306.]

Besides the Roman lady who died of joy when she saw her son safe back from the defeat at Cannae, and Sophocles, and Dionysius the Tyrant, who died of joy, and Thalna, who died in Corsica reading the news of the honours the Roman Senate had decreed in his favour — we have, even in our own time, the example of Pope Leo X, who on hearing of the taking of Milan (a thing he had wanted with all his heart) was seized with so sudden an excess of joy that he immediately fell into a fever and died. And for a more striking testimony to the weakness of our human nature, it is recorded by the ancients that Diodorus the dialectician dropped dead on the spot, from sheer overwhelming shame at not having been able, in his own school and in the presence of a great audience, to extricate himself from a nice argument that had been put to him. For my part, I am very little subject to these violent passions; I am naturally of a stubborn cast of mind, which by reasoning I make harder and stronger every day.

title: That our affections carry themselves beyond us
paragraphs: Those who accuse mankind of the folly of gaping after future things, and advise us to make use of the present and rest content with it on the ground that we have no grip on what is to come, even less than we have on what is past, have put their finger on the most universal of human errors — if it can be called an error, since nature herself has put it in us, for the continuation of her own work, planting in us, among other things, this deceiving imagination, more jealous of our acting than afraid of our knowing.

We are never with ourselves; we are always somewhere beyond. Fear, desire, hope keep pushing us toward the future, and meanwhile rob us of the sense and consideration of what is, to amuse us with the thought of what shall be — even when we shall be no more.
"Calamitosus est animus futuri anxius."
["The mind anxious about the future is miserable." — Seneca, Epist., 98.]

We find this great rule repeated often in Plato: "Do your own work, and know yourself." Each part contains all our duty between them, and each in its way involves the other; for whoever will do his own work properly will find that his first lesson is to know what he is and what is proper to him, and whoever rightly understands himself will never mistake another man's work for his own — he will love and improve himself above all else, refuse superfluous employments, and put aside all useless thoughts and propositions. As folly, on one side, even if it had everything it desired, would never be content, so wisdom, settling for what is present, is never dissatisfied with itself. Epicurus excuses his sages from all foresight and care of the future.

Among the laws relating to the dead, I think this a very sound one: that the actions of princes be examined after their death. They are equal with the laws, when not above them, and therefore what justice could not inflict on their persons it is only reasonable should fall on their reputations and on the estates of their successors — things we often value above life itself. This is a custom of singular advantage to the countries that use it, and one all good princes should welcome, for they have reason to be offended that the memories of the wicked should be treated with the same reverence as their own. We owe submission and obedience to all our kings, good or bad alike, for that has to do with their office; but esteem and affection are owed only to their virtue. Grant to political government that we endure unworthy rulers with patience, conceal their vices, and lend our recommendation to their indifferent actions while their authority still needs our support. But once the relation of prince and subject is over, there is no reason to deny our true opinions their voice, in the name of liberty and common justice; least of all to deny good subjects the glory of having served reverently and faithfully a prince whose imperfections they knew very well, since that would be to deprive posterity of a useful example. And those who, out of some private obligation, unjustly take up and defend the memory of a faulty prince serve a private interest at the cost of public justice. Livy says, very truly, that the language of men brought up in courts is always full of vain display and false witness: every one indifferently exalts his own master and stretches his praise to the utmost extent of virtue and sovereign greatness. Some may condemn the boldness of those two soldiers who answered Nero so roundly to his face. The one, asked why he hated him, said: "I loved you while you were worth it. Since you have become a parricide, an incendiary, a player, and a coachman, I hate you as you deserve." And the other, asked why he had tried to kill him, said: "Because I could think of no other remedy against your endless mischief." But the public, universal testimony given of Nero after his death (and which will go on being given of him, and of every other wicked prince like him, to all posterity) of his tyrannies and abominable conduct — who, in his sound judgment, can object to it?

I am offended that in a government as sacred as that of the Lacedaemonians there should have been mixed in so hypocritical a ceremony at the funeral of their kings — where all their allies, all their neighbours, and all kinds and ranks of men and women, including their slaves, cut and slashed their foreheads as a sign of grief, crying and lamenting that this king (even if he had been as wicked as the devil himself) was the best they had ever had. The effect is to attribute to his rank the praise that belongs only to merit, and that is properly owed to supreme worth even when it is found in the lowest and least placed subject.

Aristotle, who must have a finger in everything, raises a question about Solon's saying that no one can be called happy until he is dead: whether someone who has lived and died according to his heart's desire, but has left a bad name behind him and a miserable line of descendants, can really be called happy. As long as we have life and movement we can carry ourselves in fancy and preoccupation wherever we please; but once we are out of being, we have no further communication with what is — and so Solon would have done better to say that no one is ever happy, since he cannot really be so until he is no more.
"Quisquam Vix radicitus e vita se tollit, et eicit; Sed facit esse sui quiddam super inscius ipse, Nec removet satis a projecto corpore sese, et Vindicat."

["Scarcely any man can, even when dying, wholly detach himself from the idea of life; in his ignorance he imagines that something of himself survives, and cannot fully separate himself from his discarded body, or set himself free of it." — Lucretius, iii. 890.]

Bertrand du Guesclin, dying at the siege of the Castle of Rancon, near Le Puy in Auvergne, the besieged were ordered after surrender to lay the keys of the place upon the dead general's body. When Bartolommeo d'Alviano, the Venetian general, happened to die in the service of the Republic at Brescia, and his body had to be carried through the territory of Verona — enemy country — most of the army was inclined to ask the Veronese for safe-conduct. Theodoro Trivulzio opposed it, preferring to force a passage by arms and risk a battle, saying it was not fitting that one who had never feared his enemies in life should seem to fear them in death. Under Greek law, in fact, anyone who applied to an enemy for a body to bury it forfeited his victory and could no longer set up a trophy, while the one applied to was reckoned the winner. By this Nicias lost the advantage he had visibly gained over the Corinthians; and Agesilaus, by the same rule, secured an advantage over the Boeotians that he had only doubtfully earned in the field.

These things might seem strange if it had not been the general practice in every age, not only to extend our concern with ourselves beyond this life, but to imagine that heaven's favour does not merely often accompany us to the grave but, after life is over, takes an interest in our ashes. There are so many ancient examples of this — leaving aside what we see in our own time — that I need not labour the point. Edward I, King of England, in his long wars against Robert, King of Scotland, had experience of how decisive his own presence in person was to the success of his enterprises, having always been victorious in whatever he undertook in person; when he was dying he bound his son by solemn oath that as soon as he was dead his body should be boiled until the flesh came off the bones, and the flesh buried while the bones were preserved to be carried with the army whenever it had to march against the Scots — as if destiny had inevitably attached victory even to his remains. John Zizka, the same man who, in defence of Wycliffe's heresies, threw the Bohemian state into turmoil, left orders that he be flayed after his death and his skin made into a drum to be carried in war against his enemies, in the belief that it would contribute to the continuation of the successes he had always had against them. In the same way, certain of the Indians, in their battles with the Spaniards, carried with them the bones of one of their captains, on account of the victories they had once won under his command. And other peoples in that same New World carry with them in war the relics of brave men who had died in battle, to fire their courage and improve their luck. In the first kind of example, what was reserved for the tomb was only the reputation earned by past achievement; in the others, an active power is still attributed to the dead.

Captain Bayard's behaviour is of a better grain. Mortally wounded by a harquebus shot and pressed to retire from the fight, he answered that he would not begin at the last gasp to turn his back on the enemy. He fought on until, feeling himself too faint to sit on his horse, he ordered his steward to set him down at the foot of a tree — but so that he might die with his face toward the enemy, which he did.

I must add another example, no less striking than any of the rest for the present matter. The Emperor Maximilian, great-grandfather of the present King Philip, was a prince in whom great and uncommon qualities were everywhere mixed, including a singular personal beauty; but he had one habit very contrary to that of other princes, who for the despatch of their most important affairs turn the close-stool into a chair of state. He would not let any of his bedchamber, however familiar, see him in that posture, and would steal aside to make water as scrupulously as a virgin, shy of letting his physician or anyone else see those parts we are accustomed to conceal. I myself — for all the unembarrassed way I talk — am naturally so modest in this that, except under the pressure of necessity or pleasure, I scarcely ever let anyone see those parts or actions custom requires us to conceal: I suffer here more constraint than I think is becoming in a man, and especially in one of my profession. Maximilian fostered this modest humour to a degree of superstition: he gave express orders in his last will that they should put drawers on him as soon as he was dead — to which, I think, he might as well have added that the man who put them on should also be blindfolded. The charge Cyrus left with his children, that neither they nor anyone else should see or touch his body once the soul had left it, I put down to some superstitious devotion of his; for both Cyrus and his historian were noted throughout their great qualities for a singular respect and reverence for religion.

I was not at all pleased by a story told me, by a man of very great quality, about a relative of mine who had given a very good account of himself in peace and war: that coming to die in extreme old age, in excessive pain from the stone, he spent the last hours of his life in an extraordinary preoccupation with the honour and ceremony of his funeral. He pressed all the men of standing who came to see him to give their word to attend him to his grave; he importuned the prince himself, who came to visit him at his last gasp, with an earnest plea that he would order his household to be there; he laid out several arguments and examples to prove this was a respect due to a man of his condition; and he seemed to die content once he had obtained the promise and laid out the order and method of his funeral parade. I have seldom heard of so persistent a vanity.

Another, contrary curiosity (and there is no shortage of examples in my own family) seems somehow akin to this one: that a man should rack his brains in his last moments to plan obsequies of so peculiarly studied a frugality as to have one servant with a lantern. I see this humour praised, and the arrangement of Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, who forbade his heirs to spend on his funeral even the common ceremonies usual on such occasions. Is it really temperance and frugality to avoid expense and pleasure when the use and knowledge of them is imperceptible to us? An easy and cheap reformation. If guidance were needed here, I would say that in this, as in every other action of life, each person ought to regulate the matter according to his fortune. The philosopher Lycon prudently told his friends to dispose of his body wherever they thought best, and as for the funeral, to make it neither too superfluous nor too mean. For my part, I would leave the ordering of this ceremony entirely to custom, and shall, when the time comes, leave it to the discretion of whoever has to do me that last office. "Totus hic locus est contemnendus in nobis, non negligendus in nostris"; and a saint said this, very holily: "Curatio funeris, conditio sepulturae: pompa exequiarum, magis sunt vivorum solatia, quam subsidia mortuorum." Which made Socrates answer Crito, who asked him at his death how he wished to be buried: "However you like." If I were to occupy myself beyond the present with this affair at all, I should be most tempted, as the highest pleasure of this kind, to imitate those who in their lifetime entertain themselves with the ceremony and honours of their own obsequies in advance, and take pleasure in looking at their own dead face in marble. Happy are they who can gratify their senses by insensibility, and live by their death.

I am ready to feel an implacable hatred for every form of popular rule, though I think it the most natural and equitable of all, every time I remember the inhuman injustice of the people of Athens, who, without any hearing or vouchsafing the men a word in their defence, put to death their brave captains just returned in triumph from a naval victory they had won over the Lacedaemonians near the Arginusae Isles — the bloodiest and most stubborn engagement the Greeks ever fought at sea. The reason: that after the victory they had pressed their advantage according to the rule of war rather than stop to collect and bury their dead. The execution is the more odious for the behaviour of Diomedon, one of the condemned and a man of eminent virtue in both politics and arms. Once the sentence had been pronounced — no audience had been allowed until then — he stepped forward to speak, and instead of pleading his own cause or arguing the impiety of so cruel a sentence, only expressed concern for his judges' welfare. He asked the gods to turn this sentence to their good, and prayed that, for his and his companions' failure to fulfil the vows they had made (which he then named) in thanks for so glorious a victory, the gods' anger might not fall on them. And so without more words he went courageously to his death.

Fortune punished them in kind a few years later. Chabrias, captain-general of their naval forces, had the better of Pollis, the Spartan admiral, at the Isle of Naxos, but lost the whole fruit of his victory, a thing of great importance to their affairs, in order not to fall under this example: rather than lose a few bodies of dead friends that were floating in the sea, he gave a host of living enemies the chance to sail away in safety — and they made the Athenians pay dearly afterwards for this unseasonable superstition.
"Quaeris, quo jaceas, post obitum, loco? Quo non nata jacent."
["You ask where you shall lie after death? Where things lie that were never born."] — Seneca, Troades, Chorus ii. 30.
This other line restores the sense of rest to a body without a soul:
"Neque sepulcrum, quo recipiatur, habeat: portum corporis, ubi, remissa humana, vita, corpus requiescat a malis."
["Let him have no tomb to receive him, no haven for his body where, life being gone, the body may rest from its troubles." — Ennius, in Cicero, Tusc. i. 44.]

As nature shows us, several dead things keep a hidden relation to life. Wine changes its flavour and colour in the cellar according to the changes and seasons of the vine it came from; and the flesh of venison alters its condition in the brine-tub, and its taste, according to the laws of the living flesh of its kind — so it is said.

title: That the soul expends its passions upon false objects, where the true are wanting
paragraphs: A gentleman of my country, terribly tormented by gout and ordered by his physicians to abstain entirely from any kind of salt meat, used to reply pleasantly that in the height of his fits he needed something to quarrel with, and that railing and cursing — one moment at the Bologna sausages, the next at the dried tongues and hams — gave him some mitigation of his pain. But seriously, just as the arm raised to strike pains us if it misses its blow and only beats the wind, and just as, for a view to be a pleasant one, the sight should not be lost and diffused in vague air but should have some bound and object to limit and frame it at a reasonable distance —
"Ventus ut amittit vires, nisi robore densa Occurrant sylvae, spatio diffusus inani."
["As the wind loses its force diffused in empty space unless in its full strength it meets a thick wood." — Lucan, iii. 362.]

— so it seems the soul, once carried away and unsettled, turns its violence upon itself if not supplied with something to resist it. It always needs an object to aim at and to work upon. Plutarch says of those who dote on little dogs and monkeys that the loving part in us, lacking a legitimate object rather than lie idle, forges and invents a false and frivolous one. And we can see that the soul, in its passions, would rather deceive itself by creating a false and fantastical subject — even one it does not really believe in — than have nothing at all to work upon. In the same way brute beasts direct their fury at the stone or weapon that has hurt them, and even take their revenge with their teeth on themselves for the injury they have received from another:
"Pannonis haud aliter, post ictum saevior ursa, Cui jaculum parva Lybis amentavit habena, Se rotat in vulnus, telumque irata receptum Impetit, et secum fugientem circuit hastam."

["So the she-bear, made fiercer by the blow from the Libyan's strap-hurled dart, turns round upon the wound and, enraged, attacks the spear lodged in her, spinning round the shaft that flies with her." — Lucan, vi. 220.]

What causes do we not invent for the misfortunes that happen to us? What is it that we do not blame, rightly or wrongly, just so we may have something to quarrel with? It is not those beautiful tresses you tear, nor the white breast you so unmercifully beat in your anger, that with a stray bullet killed your beloved brother — quarrel with something else. Livy, speaking of the Roman army in Spain, says that when news came of the loss of the two brothers, their great captains:
"Flere omnes repente, et offensare capita."
["All at once they wept and tore their hair." — Livy, xxv. 37.]

It is a common reflex. And the philosopher Bion said wittily of the king who tore his hair out by the handful in grief: "Does this man think baldness is a remedy for sorrow?" Who has not seen peevish gamblers chewing and swallowing the cards or the dice in revenge for the loss of their money? Xerxes whipped the sea and sent a written challenge to Mount Athos; Cyrus kept a whole army at work for several days to take his revenge on the river Gyndes, for the fright it had given him in crossing; and Caligula tore down a beautiful palace because his mother had once enjoyed herself there.

I remember a story going around when I was a boy — that one of our neighbouring kings, having received a blow from the hand of God, swore he would have his revenge, and to that end issued a proclamation that for the next ten years no one should pray to Him, or so much as mention Him throughout his dominions, or, as far as his authority went, believe in Him; by which they meant to paint not so much the folly as the vainglory of the nation the tale was told about. The two vices always travel together, but in truth such actions have in them still more presumption than want of wit. Augustus Caesar, having been tossed about by a storm at sea, took to defying Neptune, and during the pomp of the Circensian games, by way of revenge, removed his statue from its place among the other deities. In which he was still less excusable than the man before him, and less so than he was again later when, having lost a battle under Quintilius Varus in Germany, in rage and despair he ran his head against the wall, crying out, "Varus, give me back my legions!" These outdo all folly, since impiety is now added to them — invading God himself, or at least Fortune, as if she had ears subject to our batteries; like the Thracians who, when it thunders or lightens, fall to shooting against heaven with Titan-like vengeance, as if by flights of arrows they meant to bring God to reason. Even though the ancient poet in Plutarch tells us —
"Point ne se faut couroucer aux affaires, Il ne leur chault de toutes nos choleres."
["We must not get angry with the gods over our affairs; they take no notice of our angers and disputes." — Plutarch.]
— still, we can never sufficiently denounce the disorderly outbursts of our minds.

title: Whether the governor of a place besieged ought himself to go out to parley
paragraphs: Quintus Marcius, the Roman legate in the war against Perseus, King of Macedon, in order to gain time to reinforce his army, put out some openings for an accommodation, by which the king was lulled into agreeing to a truce of several days — long enough to give his enemy the opportunity and leisure to recruit fresh forces, which was the cause of the king's final ruin. Yet the elder senators, mindful of their forefathers' ways, condemned this procedure as a falling-off from their ancient practice, which, they said, was to fight by valour, not by trickery, surprises, or night-encounters; not by feigned flight or sudden rallies to overcome the enemy; and never to make war without first proclaiming it, often setting both the hour and the place of battle. It was on this generous principle that they handed Pyrrhus's treacherous physician back to him, and the Etruscans' disloyal schoolmaster back to them. This was a truly Roman procedure, with no resemblance to Greek subtlety or to Punic cunning, where it was reckoned a less glorious victory to overcome by force than by fraud. Deceit may serve in a pinch, but only that man can truly admit he has been beaten who knows he has been overcome neither by policy nor by accident, but by sheer valour, man to man, in fair and just war. It clearly appears from the talk of those good old senators that this fine line had not yet found its way among them:
"Dolus, an virtus, quis in hoste requirat?"
["Who asks, in dealing with an enemy, whether by valour or by stratagem?" — Aeneid, ii. 390.]
The Achaeans, says Polybius, abhorred every kind of double-dealing in war, and did not count it a victory unless the enemy's courage had been fairly subdued.
"Eam vir sanctus et sapiens sciet veram esse victoriam, quae, salva fide et integra dignitate, parabitur." And another says:
"Vosne velit, an me, regnare hera, quidve ferat, fors virtute experiamur."
["Whether you or I shall reign, or what shall happen, let us decide by valour." — Cicero, De Officiis, i. 12.]

In the kingdom of Ternate, among nations we loosely call barbarians, they have a custom never to begin a war without first proclaiming it, and adding a full declaration of what they have to fight with — how many men, what ammunition, what offensive and defensive arms; but once that is done, if the enemy will not yield and come to terms, they consider it lawful to use, without reproach, any means that may help them win.

The ancient Florentines were so far from seeking advantage over their enemies by surprise that they always gave them a month's warning before they took the field, by the continual tolling of a bell they called the Martinella.

For our part, we are less scrupulous about such things, and grant the honour of war to whoever profits by it. We say, with Lysander, that "where the lion's skin is too short, we must eke it out with a piece of the fox's," and the most common openings for surprise come from this practice. There are no moments when a commander needs to be more on his guard than during parleys and negotiations for accommodation. From which it has become a general rule among the soldiers of recent times that the governor of a place under siege should never go out to parley. It was for breaking this rule that, in our fathers' day, the Seigneurs de Montmord and de l'Assigny, defending Mousson against the Count of Nassau, were so harshly criticised. Even so, it might be excusable in a governor who, when he goes out, does so in a way that keeps the safety and the advantage on his own side — as Count Guido di Rangone did at Reggio (if we believe Du Bellay; Guicciardini says it was Guicciardini himself) when the Seigneur de l'Escut came up to parley. He stepped so little away from his fort that, when a disturbance broke out during the parley, not only did Monsieur de l'Escut and his party — who had advanced with him — find themselves much the weaker (so much so that Alessandro Trivulzio was killed there), but l'Escut himself was glad to follow the count and, trusting to his honour, take cover behind the walls of the town from the danger of the shot.

Eumenes, shut up in the city of Nora by Antigonus and pressed by him to come out and speak with him (since, as Antigonus put it, he was the greater of the two and now had the advantage), returned this noble answer: "Tell him that I shall never reckon any man greater than myself while I have my sword in my hand," and he would not consent to come out until Antigonus had, at his own demand, delivered up his nephew Ptolomeus as a hostage.

And yet some have done very well going out in person to parley, on the assailant's word — witness Henri de Vaux, a cavalier of Champagne, who, besieged by the English in the castle of Commercy, found that Bartholomew de Brunes, the besieging commander, had sapped so much of the castle from outside that nothing remained but to set fire to the props and bury the besieged under the ruins. Brunes asked Henri to come out and speak with him for his own good, which he did with three others in company. His destruction was made plain to him, and feeling himself singularly obliged to his enemy he and his garrison surrendered themselves to his discretion. As soon as the mine was fired and the props began to fail, the castle was instantly blown up from its foundations, not one stone left upon another.

I can — and do — quite easily trust the word of another; but I should be very unwilling to do so in a case like this, where it might be judged to be the effect of despair and want of courage rather than a voluntary act done out of confidence and security in the good faith of the man I had to deal with.

title: That the hour of parley is dangerous
paragraphs: Even so, I recently saw at Mussidan, a place not far from my house, that those who had been driven out from there by our army, and others of their party, complained loudly of treachery: during a negotiation, and at the very moment their deputies were in talks, they were taken by surprise and cut to pieces. In another age, perhaps, that might have looked like foul play. But, as I have just been saying, the practice of arms in our day is quite another matter, and one cannot afford to trust an enemy until the treaty is finally sealed. Even then the victor has enough trouble keeping his word, so hazardous is it to entrust the observance of a man's pledged faith to a town that has surrendered on easy and favourable terms, to the licence of a victorious army, and to let the soldier in with his blood still up.

Lucius Aemilius Regillus, the Roman praetor, having wasted his time trying to take the city of Phocaea by force because of the extraordinary courage with which the inhabitants defended themselves, agreed at last to receive them as friends of the people of Rome and to enter the town as he would enter a confederate city, with no kind of hostility — and gave them all the assurances they asked for. But once he had, for the greater pomp, brought his whole army in with him, it was no longer in his power, however hard he tried, to restrain his men. Avarice and revenge trampled both his authority and all military discipline underfoot, and he saw a considerable part of the city sacked and ruined before his eyes.

Cleomenes used to say that whatever harm a man could do his enemy in wartime was above justice and not accountable to it in the sight of gods or men. So, having concluded a seven-day truce with the Argives, he fell on them on the third night when they were all asleep and put them to the sword, alleging that no nights had been mentioned in the truce. But the gods punished this clever treachery.

In a time of parley too, and while the citizens were relying on their safe-conduct, the city of Casilinum was taken by surprise — and that in the age of the most upright captains and the most rigorous Roman military discipline. For it is not denied that we may, in due time and place, take advantage of an enemy's lack of understanding as well as of his lack of courage.

And undoubtedly war has by nature many privileges that look reasonable even when they go against reason. So here the rule fails — "Neminem id agere ut ex alterius praedetur inscitia." But I am astonished at the great liberty Xenophon allows in such cases, both by precept and by the example of his ideal commander's many exploits. He is an author of very great authority on such matters, I admit, being himself both a great captain and a leading philosopher among Socrates's disciples; and yet I cannot agree to the licence he grants in everything, in all places.

Monsieur d'Aubigny, besieging Capua and pounding it with a furious battery, found that Signor Fabrizio Colonna, the governor of the town, had begun a parley from a bastion. While his soldiers, meanwhile, slackened their guard, our men slipped in and put them all to the sword. And more recently, at Yvoy, Signor Giuliano Romero, playing the novice by going out to parley with the Constable, found his place taken at his return. But, that we should not get off scot-free, the Marquess of Pescara, laying siege to Genoa where Duke Ottaviano Fregoso commanded under our protection, had the terms between them so far advanced that the matter was looked on as done and on the point of being concluded — and then the Spaniards slipped in and used this treachery as an outright victory. And since, at Ligny in Barrois, where the Count de Brienne was in command, when the emperor in person besieged the place and Bertheville, the count's lieutenant, went out to parley, the town was taken while he was negotiating.
"Fu il vincer sempremai laudabil cosa, Vincasi o per fortuna, o per ingegno,"
["Victory is always praiseworthy, whether it is gained by fortune or by skill." — Ariosto, xv. 1.]

But the philosopher Chrysippus held the opposite view, and I share it. He used to say that those who run a race ought to put all their force into what they are doing and run as fast as they can; but that it is by no means fair to lay a hand on a rival to slow him, or stick out a leg to trip him up. And more generous still was the answer of the great Alexander to Polypercon, who urged him to take advantage of the night's darkness to fall on Darius: "Not at all," he said; "it is not for such a man as I am to steal a victory. Malo me fortunae poeniteat, quam victoria pudeat."
"Atque idem fugientem haud est dignatus Oroden Sternere, nec jacta caecum dare cuspide vulnus Obvius, adversoque occurrit, seque viro vir Contulit, haud furto melior, sed fortibus armis."

["He did not deign to strike Orodes down as he fled, nor to give him a hidden wound with a hurled spear, but caught up with him, faced him, and met him man to man — superior, not by stealth, but by valiant arms." — Aeneid, x. 732.]

title: That the intention is judge of our actions
paragraphs: There is a saying that death discharges us of all our obligations. I know some who have taken it in another sense. Henry VII of England agreed with Don Philip, son of the emperor Maximilian — or, to give him a more honourable title, father of the Emperor Charles V — that Philip should hand over the Duke of Suffolk of the White Rose, Henry's enemy, who had fled into the Low Countries. Philip duly did so, but on condition that Henry would not attempt the duke's life. But when Henry came to die, he commanded his son in his last will to put the duke to death as soon as he himself was dead. And lately, in the tragedy the Duke of Alva put on for us at Brussels in the persons of the Counts Horn and Egmont, there were several striking moments. One in particular: Count Egmont (on whose word and faith Count Horn had come and surrendered himself to the Duke of Alva) earnestly asked to be allowed to mount the scaffold first, so that death might discharge him of the obligation he had given the other. In that case it seems to me that death did not in fact acquit the former of his promise, and that the latter was discharged from it without dying. We cannot be bound beyond what we are able to perform, since effect and performance are not really in our power: indeed the only thing we are masters of is the will, and on the will, by necessity, all the rules and the whole duty of mankind are founded and established. Count Egmont, therefore, regarding his soul and his will as still bound by his promise even though he had not the power to make it good, would no doubt have been absolved of his duty even if he had outlived the other. But the King of England, who deliberately and with full intent broke his faith, was no more to be excused for putting off the execution of his infidelity until after his death than the mason in Herodotus, who kept the secret of his master the King of Egypt's treasure inviolate during his lifetime but at his own death revealed it to his children.

I have noticed several in my own time who, convicted in their consciences of unjustly holding on to other people's goods, have tried to make amends in their will, after their deaths. They might as well do nothing — either taking so much time over so pressing a matter, or trying to make a wrong good with so little inconvenience and loss to themselves. They owe over and above; and the more strict and uncomfortable their payment is to themselves, the more just and meritorious is their restitution. Penitence calls for some penalty. Worse still are those who have kept their malice against a neighbour hidden all their lives and reserve it for their last gasp. They show little regard for their own honour, by provoking the offended party in their memory, and little for their conscience, by being unable, even out of respect for death itself, to let their malice die with them but instead extending the life of their hatred beyond their own life. Unjust judges, who delay judgment until they no longer have any knowledge of the cause! For my own part, I shall take care, if I can, that my death reveal nothing my life has not first and openly declared.

title: Of idleness
paragraphs: Just as we see that pieces of ground long left idle and untilled, once they grow rich and fertile through rest, abound with and spend their virtue on producing countless kinds of weeds and wild herbs of no use — and that, to make them perform their proper office, we must cultivate and prepare them to receive seeds proper to our service; just as we see women who, without ever knowing a man, sometimes bring forth, of themselves, shapeless lumps of inanimate flesh, but who to bring about a natural and perfect generation must be served by another kind of seed — even so it is with minds, which, if not applied to some specific study to fix and restrain them, run riot in a thousand extravagances, drifting endlessly here and there in the vague expanse of imagination —
"Sicut aqua tremulum labris ubi lumen ahenis, Sole repercussum, aut radiantis imagine lunae, Omnia pervolitat late loca; jamque sub auras Erigitur, summique ferit laquearia tecti."

["As when in brazen vats of water the trembling light, reflected from the sun or from the image of the radiant moon, flits swiftly over every place around, and is now darted up on high to strike the panels of the ceiling overhead." — Aeneid, viii. 22.]
— and in this wild agitation there is no folly and no idle fancy they do not light upon:
"Velut aegri somnia, vanae Finguntur species."
["Like a sick man's dreams, creating empty phantoms." — Horace, Ars Poetica, 7.]
The soul that has no settled aim loses itself, for, as it is said —
"Quisquis ubique habitat, Maxime, nusquam habitat."
["He who lives everywhere, lives nowhere." — Martial, vii. 73.]

When I lately retired to my own house, determined as far as I could to avoid any kind of involvement in affairs and to spend in privacy and peace the little time I have left to live, I imagined I could do my mind no greater favour than to leave it at full leisure to entertain and divert itself, and that I now hoped it might do so, being by this time more settled and more mature. But I find —
"Variam semper dant otia mentem,"
["Leisure always breeds shifting thoughts." — Lucan, iv. 704.]

— that, quite the contrary, it is like a horse that has broken from its rider and runs off into a much wilder career than any horseman would have urged on it, and it produces in me so many chimeras and fantastic monsters, one after another, without order or design, that, the better to contemplate at leisure their strangeness and absurdity, I have begun to set them down in writing, hoping in time to make my mind ashamed of itself.

title: Of liars
paragraphs: There is no living man whom it would less become to speak from memory than me, for I have hardly any at all, and I do not think the world contains another so amazingly treacherous as mine. My other faculties are all sufficiently ordinary and middling; but in this one I think myself quite rare and singular, deserving to be famous for it. Beyond the natural inconvenience I suffer because of it (for, given how necessary the use of memory is, Plato was right to call it a great and powerful goddess), in my part of the country, when they want to say that a man has no sense, they say he has no memory; and when I complain that mine is defective, they do not believe me, and reprove me as though I were calling myself a fool — failing to see the difference between memory and understanding, which only makes things worse for me. But they do me wrong, for experience daily shows the opposite: that a strong memory is commonly paired with weak judgment. They also wrong me — me who am as perfect in nothing as in friendship — by making the very words that complain of my infirmity portray me as ungrateful. They draw my feelings into question on the basis of my memory, and from a natural imperfection make out a defect of conscience. "He has forgotten," says one, "this request, or that promise; he no longer remembers his friends; he has forgotten to say or do or hide this or that thing for my sake." And I am indeed apt to forget many things, but to neglect anything a friend has committed to my charge — that I never do. It ought to be enough that I feel the misery and inconvenience of it, without being branded with malice, a vice as contrary to my temper as anything could be.

Still, I take these comforts from my infirmity. First, that it is an evil from which I have chiefly found reason to correct a worse one that would easily have grown on me — namely, ambition, a fault that is intolerable in anyone taking on public affairs. As similar examples in the course of nature show, she has strengthened me in my other faculties in proportion as she has left me unfurnished in this one; otherwise I should have been apt to rest my mind and judgment, by default, on the bare reports of other men, never setting them to work on their own force, if the inventions and opinions of others had been continually available to me through the convenience of memory. By this means too I am not so talkative, for the storeroom of memory is always better stocked with material than the storeroom of invention. If mine had been faithful, I would by now have deafened all my friends with my chatter — the subjects rousing and stirring up the small faculty I have for handling and using them, warming and stretching out my discourse — which would be a pity, as I have observed in several of my close friends who, with their memories supplying them a complete and full view of things, begin their narrative so far back, and clutter it with so many irrelevant circumstances, that even when the story is a good one they manage to spoil it. If it is not a good one, you are left to curse either the strength of their memory or the weakness of their judgment. It is a hard thing to close off a discourse and cut it short once it is started; there is nothing in which the strength of a horse shows itself more than in a clean and sudden stop. I see even those who keep to the point, but cannot stop short in their career; for while they are casting about for a handsome cadence to finish with, they go on at random, wandering off into trivialities, like men staggering on weak legs. Above all, old men who keep the memory of things past, and forget how often they have told them, are dangerous company; I have known stories from the mouth of a man of very great quality, very pleasant in themselves, become wearisome by being repeated a hundred times over to the same people.

Secondly, this way I remember the injuries I have received less. As the ancient said, I should need a register of injuries, or a prompter, like Darius, who, so as not to forget the offence he had received from the people of Athens, had a page repeat in his ear three times every time he sat down to dinner: "Sir, remember the Athenians." And then again, the places I revisit, and the books I read over again, still smile on me with a fresh novelty.

It is not without good reason that it is said "that a man who has not a good memory should never take up the trade of lying." I know perfectly well that grammarians distinguish between speaking an untruth and lying, and say that to speak an untruth is to say something that is false but that we believe to be true, while the definition of the verb "to lie" in Latin (from which our French is taken) is to say something we know in our conscience to be untrue; and it is only this last sort of liar I am speaking of here. Now these either invent outright the untruths they tell, or alter and disguise a true story so completely that it ends in a lie. When they alter and disguise the same story to fit their own fancy, it is very hard for them, sooner or later, not to be tripped up; since the real truth of the matter, having taken first possession of the memory and lodged there through the channels of knowledge and study, will not easily refuse to present itself to the imagination and crowd out the falsehood, which cannot have so sure and settled a footing there as the other; and the circumstances of the first, true knowledge, always running in their minds, will make them forget those that are illegitimate and forged by their own fancy. When they wholly invent, since there is no contrary impression to push against their invention, there seems to be less danger of stumbling — and yet even this, because it is an empty body without anything to anchor it, is very apt to escape the memory if it is not very firmly fixed. I have had very entertaining experience of this at the expense of men who make a business of fitting their speech to the affair they have in hand, or to the humour of the great folk they are addressing; for the circumstances to which these men readily enslave their good faith and conscience being subject to several changes, their language has to vary accordingly. So it happens that of the same thing they tell one man it is this, and another that it is that, giving it different colours — and these men, if they ever happen to compare notes and discover the trick, what becomes of this fine art? To which one should add that they must, of necessity, very often ridiculously trip themselves up; for what memory could possibly retain so many different shapes as they have forged about one and the same subject? I have known many in my time very ambitious of the reputation for this sort of cleverness, but they do not see that if they get the reputation, the effect can no longer follow.

In plain truth, lying is an accursed vice. We are men, and we have no tie on one another except by our word. If we really understood the horror and gravity of it, we should pursue lying with fire and sword, and more justly than other crimes. I see that parents commonly, and rather unwisely, correct their children for little innocent faults, and torment them over trifles that leave no impression and have no consequence; whereas, in my opinion, lying, and at a lower level, obstinacy, are the faults that should be severely thrashed out of them, both in their infancy and as they grow. Otherwise they grow up and grow worse with them, and once a tongue has got the trick of lying, it is unimaginable how impossible it is to reclaim. Hence we see some men, otherwise quite honest, so subject and enslaved to this vice. I have an honest lad for my tailor whom I have never once known to tell a truth, not even when it would have been to his advantage. If falsehood, like truth, had only one face, we should be on better terms with it, for we should then take for certain the opposite of whatever the liar said. But the reverse of truth has a hundred thousand faces and a boundless field, without limit. The Pythagoreans hold that good is certain and finite, and evil infinite and uncertain. There are a thousand ways to miss the mark; there is only one way to hit it. For my own part, I have such a horror of this vice that I am not sure I could prevail on my conscience to save myself from the most evident and extreme danger by a blatant and solemn lie. An ancient father says that "a dog we know is better company than a man whose language we do not understand."
"Ut externus alieno pene non sit hominis vice."
["So that a foreigner is almost not a man at all to us." — Pliny, Natural History, vii. 1.]
And how much less sociable is false speech than silence?

King Francis I boasted that he had by this means tied up Francesco Taverna, the ambassador of Francesco Sforza, Duke of Milan — a man very famous in his day for his skill in talking. This gentleman had been sent to excuse his master to His Majesty in a very serious business, which was this: the king, in order to keep up some intelligence in Italy, out of which he had lately been driven, and particularly with the Duchy of Milan, had thought it convenient to keep a gentleman of his own on hand with the duke — an ambassador in effect, but in outward appearance a private person who was supposed to be residing there on his own affairs. The duke, being much more dependent on the emperor (especially while he was negotiating his marriage with the emperor's niece, daughter of the King of Denmark, who is now the dowager of Lorraine), could not show any open dealings or conferences with us without serious risk. For this commission, one Merveille, a Milanese gentleman and an equerry of the king, was thought very suitable, and was sent there with private credentials and instructions as ambassador, along with other letters of recommendation to the duke concerning his own private affairs, the better to mask and colour the business. He was so long at that court that the emperor at last got wind of his real employment there — which was the cause, we suppose, of what followed: under pretext of some murder, his trial was dispatched in two days, and his head was struck off in prison at night. Messire Francesco arrived in France prepared with a long counterfeit account of the affair (for the king had applied to all the princes of Christendom, as well as to the duke himself, to demand satisfaction) and was given his audience at the morning council. There, after he had laid out several plausible justifications of the fact in support of his case — that his master had never looked on Merveille as anything but a private gentleman and his own subject, who was there only on his own business, and had never lived under any other character; absolutely denying that he had ever heard he was a member of the king's household, or that His Majesty so much as knew him, so far was he from taking him for an ambassador — the king, pressing him in turn with several objections and demands and challenging him from every side, tripped him up at last by asking, then, why the execution had been carried out at night, and as it were by stealth. At which the poor confounded ambassador, the more elegantly to extricate himself, replied that the duke would have been very loath, out of respect for His Majesty, to have such an execution carried out by day. One can imagine how he was scolded when he got home, for having so grossly tripped in the presence of a prince of so delicate a nose as King Francis.

Pope Julius II, having sent an ambassador to the King of England to stir him up against King Francis, had his ambassador heard. Before he would give an answer, the king urged the difficulties he would meet in setting on foot so great a preparation as would be needed to attack so powerful a king, and gave his reasons. The ambassador very unseasonably replied that he too had considered the same difficulties and had laid them before the pope. From this saying, so directly contrary to the matter in hand and the business he had come for (which was simply to incite the king to war), the King of England first drew the conclusion (which he later found to be true) that this ambassador, in his own heart, was on the French side. He notified the pope, the ambassador's estate was confiscated at his return, and he himself only narrowly escaped losing his head.

title: Of quick or slow speech
paragraphs: "Onc ne furent a touts toutes graces donnees."
["All graces were never given to any one man." — A line from one of La Brebis's sonnets.]

So we see in the gift of eloquence, where some have such a facility and quickness — what we call a ready wit — that they are always primed for any occasion and never caught off guard, while others, heavier and slower, never risk saying anything they have not long premeditated and taken great pains to prepare.

Just as we teach young ladies the sports and exercises best fitted to show off the grace and beauty of those parts where their chief charm and perfection lie, so it should be with these two advantages of eloquence which the lawyers and preachers of our age principally lay claim to. If I were worthy to advise, the slow speaker, it seems to me, would be better suited to the pulpit and the other to the bar — for the preacher's office naturally allows him all the leisure he might want to prepare himself, and his career runs in an even, uninterrupted line, with no break or stop, whereas the pleader's business and interest compels him to enter the lists on every occasion, and the unexpected objections and replies of his opponent throw him out of his course and force him, on the instant, to think up new and extempore answers and defences. Yet at the meeting between Pope Clement and King Francis at Marseilles, it happened quite the contrary: Monsieur Poyet, a man who had spent his whole life at the bar and had the highest reputation for eloquence, was charged with making the address to the pope. Having so long meditated it beforehand that, they say, he brought it ready-made with him from Paris, on the very day it was to be delivered the pope, fearing that something might be said that would give offence to the other princes' ambassadors who were attending him there, sent word to the king of the line he thought best suited to the time and place — quite another thing, as it happened, from what Monsieur de Poyet had taken so much trouble over. So that the fine speech he had prepared was no use, and he had to come up with another on the spot, which, finding himself unable to do, Cardinal du Bellay had to step in and perform that office. The pleader's part is no doubt much harder than the preacher's, and yet, in my view, we see in France more passable lawyers than preachers. It seems that wit's nature is to be prompt and sudden in its operations, while judgment is more deliberate and slow. But he who stays totally silent for want of leisure to prepare himself to speak well, and he whom leisure does not help to better speech, are equally unfortunate.

It is said of Severus Cassius that he spoke best extempore, that he owed more to fortune than to his own diligence; that it was an advantage to him to be interrupted in speaking, and that his opponents were afraid to provoke him, lest his anger should redouble his eloquence. I know from experience a temperament of nature so impatient of any tedious and elaborate preparation that, unless it goes frankly and gaily about its work, it cannot do anything to purpose. We say of certain compositions that they smell of the oil and the lamp, because of a certain rough harshness that laborious handling stamps on whatever it has been used on. Beyond this, the anxiety of doing well, and the kind of straining and striving of a mind too far stretched and overbent on its task, breaks and frustrates itself like water that, by the force of its own pressing violence and abundance, cannot find a ready way out through the neck of a bottle or a narrow sluice. In the kind of nature I am now speaking of, there is this too — that it would not be disordered and stimulated by such passions as the fury of Cassius (such a motion would be too violent and rough); it would not be jostled, but coaxed; it would be roused and warmed by unexpected, sudden, and accidental occasions. Left to itself, it flags and languishes; agitation alone gives it grace and vigour. I am always at my worst in my own possession, and when wholly at my own disposal: chance has more claim on whatever comes from me than I do; occasion, company, and even the very rising and falling of my own voice draw more out of my mind than I can find when I sound and apply it by myself. So the things I say are better than those I write, if either were worth choosing where neither is worth much. This also happens to me: that I do not find myself where I look for myself, and I hit on things more by chance than by any active search of my own judgment. I sometimes happen to write something that strikes me as neat and lively, though it will appear dull and heavy to someone else — but enough of these fine compliments; every man talks like this of himself, according to his talent. When I come to speak, however, I am already so lost that I do not know what I was about to say, and on these occasions a stranger has often spotted it before me. If I made an erasure every time this inconvenience overtook me, I should leave nothing standing; occasion, on some other day, will lay the thought as plain to me as the light, and make me wonder why I should have hesitated.

title: Of prognostications
paragraphs: As to oracles, it is certain that a good while before the coming of Jesus Christ they had begun to lose their credit. Cicero, for instance, was at a loss to find the cause of their decay, and uses these words:
"Cur isto modo jam oracula Delphis non eduntur, non modo nostra aetate, sed jam diu; ut nihil possit esse contemptius?"

["Why is it that the Delphic oracles are no longer uttered as they once were — and not just in our age, but for a long time now, so that nothing could be in greater contempt?" — Cicero, De Divinatione, ii. 57.]

But as to the other prognostics — those drawn from the dissection of sacrificial animals (which is why Plato, in part, attributes a natural constitution to the intestines of the animals themselves), or from the scratching of poultry, the flight of birds —
"Aves quasdam . . . rerum augurandarum causa natas esse putamus."
["We hold that some kinds of birds were created on purpose for augury." — Cicero, De Natura Deorum, ii. 64.]
claps of thunder, the overflowing of rivers —
"Multa cernunt Aruspices, multa Augures provident, multa oraculis declarantur, multa vaticinationibus, multa somniis, multa portentis."
["The aruspices see many things, the augurs foresee many things; many are announced by oracles, many by prophecies, many by dreams, many by portents." — Cicero, De Natura Deorum, ii. 65.]

— and other like things, on which antiquity founded most of its public and private undertakings, our religion has wholly abolished them. And though there still remain among us certain practices of divination by the stars, by spirits, by people's faces and complexions, by dreams and the like (a striking example of the wild itch of our nature to grasp at and anticipate future things, as though we had not enough to do digesting the present) —

"Cur hanc tibi, rector Olympi, Sollicitis visum mortalibus addere curam, Noscant venturas ut dira per omina clades?... Sit subitum, quodcumque paras; sit coeca futuri Mens hominum fati, liceat sperare timenti."

["Why, ruler of Olympus, has it pleased you to add this burden to anxious mortals, that they should know future disasters through dire omens?... Let whatever you are preparing be sudden. Let the mind of men be blind to fate in store. Let the fearful at least be allowed to hope." — Lucan, ii. 14.]
"Ne utile quidem est scire quid futurum sit; miserum est enim, nihil proficientem angi,"
["It is not even useful to know what is going to happen; it is a wretched thing to be tormented to no purpose." — Cicero, De Natura Deorum, iii. 6.]

— yet they carry far less authority now than they used to. Which makes all the more remarkable the case of Francesco, Marquis of Saluzzo, lieutenant to King Francis I in his ultramontane army, much favoured and respected at our court, and beholden to the king's bounty for the very marquisate itself, which had been forfeited by his brother. With no real provocation given him, and with his own affection set against any such disloyalty, he let himself be terrified, as the report ran, by the fine forecasts that were being put out everywhere in favour of the Emperor Charles V, and to our disadvantage — especially in Italy, where these foolish prophecies were so far believed that at Rome large sums of money were being wagered on the returns when the prognostics came true, so sure were they of our ruin. Having often bewailed to those of his closest acquaintance the disasters he saw bound to fall on the Crown of France and on the friends he had at that court, he revolted and went over to the other side — to his own misfortune, however, whatever stars were ruling at the time. But he carried himself in this affair like a man pulled by different passions: with towns and forces in his hands, the enemy's army under Antonio de Leyva close by him, and we suspecting nothing of his design, it had been in his power to do far more than he did. We lost no men through this faithlessness of his, nor any town except Fossano, and that only after a long siege and a brave defence.
"Prudens futuri temporis exitum Caliginosa nocte premit Deus, Ridetque, si mortalis ultra Fas trepidat."
["A wise God covers the outcome of future time in dark night, and laughs at the mortal who frets beyond what is right." — Horace, Odes, iii. 29.]
"Ille potens sui Laetusque deget, cui licet in diem Dixisse vixi! cras vel atra Nube polum pater occupato, Vel sole puro."
["He lives master of himself and happy who can say, as each day passes, 'I have lived' — whether tomorrow our Father covers the sky with black cloud or with clear sun." — Horace, Odes, iii. 29.]
"Laetus in praesens animus; quod ultra est, Oderit curare."
["A mind happy in the present moment will hate to worry about what lies beyond." — Horace, Odes, ii. 16.]
And those who take this saying in the opposite sense interpret it badly:
"Ista sic reciprocantur, ut et si divinatio sit, dii sint; et si dii sint, sit divinatio."
["These two things are so connected that, if there is divination, there must be gods; and if there are gods, there must be divination." — Cicero, De Divinatione, i. 6.]
Pacuvius is wiser by far —
"Nam istis, qui linguam avium intelligunt, Plusque ex alieno jecore sapiunt, quam ex suo, Magis audiendum, quam auscultandum, censeo."

["As for those who understand the language of birds, and who get more wisdom from another animal's liver than from their own, I think they are more worth listening to than worth heeding." — Cicero, De Divinatione, i. 57, quoting Pacuvius.]

The famous art of divination among the Tuscans began like this: a labourer, striking deep into the earth with his ploughshare, saw the demi-god Tages rise up, with an infant's face but armed with mature and senile wisdom. On the rumour of this, all the people came running to see the sight, and his words and science — containing the principles and means of attaining this art — were recorded and kept for many ages. A birth in keeping with its later course. For my part, I would sooner regulate my affairs by the throw of a die than by such idle and empty dreams. And indeed, in every republic, a good share of the government has always been left to chance. Plato, in the civil polity he models on his own fancy, leaves it to decide several matters of great importance, and is willing, among other things, that marriages should be assigned by lot; he attaches such weight to this accidental choice as to require that the children born in such weddings be brought up in the country, and that those born in any other wedding be cast out as illegitimate and base. He adds, however, that if any of those exiles, as they grow, give signs of merit, they may be recalled; and that some of those who were kept may, in the same way, be exiled if they show little promise as they grow up.

I see some who are mightily given to studying and citing their almanacs, and produce them to us as an authority whenever something has fallen out aptly; and it is hardly possible that these alleged authorities, sometimes, will not stumble on a truth among an infinity of lies.
"Quis est enim, qui totum diem jaculans non aliquando collineet?"
["Who is there, indeed, who, shooting at a butt all day, will not sometimes hit the mark?" — Cicero, De Divinatione, ii. 59.]

I think no better of them for some such accidental hit. There would be more certainty about it if there were a rule, and a truth, of always lying. Besides, no one keeps a record of their flimflams and false prognostics, since they are infinite and commonplace; but if they chance upon a single truth, that makes a mighty noise as being rare, incredible, and prodigious. So Diogenes, nicknamed the Atheist, answered the man in Samothrace who showed him in the temple the various offerings and paintings of those who had escaped shipwreck and said to him: "You who think the gods take no care of human things, what do you say to so many people preserved from death by their particular favour?" "Why," Diogenes answered, "the pictures aren't here of those who were drowned — who are by far the greater number."

Cicero observes that of all the philosophers who have acknowledged a deity, only Xenophanes of Colophon has tried to root out every kind of divination — which makes it less of a wonder if we have now and then seen some of our princes, sometimes to their own cost, lean too heavily on these vanities. I would have given anything to see with my own eyes those two great marvels: the book of Joachim, the Calabrian abbot, which foretold all the future popes, with their names and characters; and that of the Emperor Leo, which prophesied all the emperors and patriarchs of Greece. This much I have witnessed myself: that in times of public confusion, men astonished at their fortune abandon their own reason and superstitiously seek out in the stars the ancient causes and warnings of their present troubles. In my time they have been so strangely successful in this that it has made me believe — this being an amusement for sharp and volatile minds — that those skilled at this knack of unfolding and untying riddles are capable of finding in any kind of writing whatever they wish. But above all, the greatest room for play is given them by the obscure, ambiguous, and fantastical gibberish of prophetic jargon, where the authors deliver nothing of clear sense but shroud everything in riddles, so that posterity may interpret and apply them according to its own fancy.

Socrates's demon may perhaps have been only a certain impulse of the will, which forced itself on him without the advice or consent of his judgment. And in a soul as enlightened as his, and so prepared by a continual exercise of wisdom and virtue, it stands to reason that these inclinations of his, however sudden and undigested, were very important and worth following. Every one of us finds in himself some image of such promptings — of a prompt, vehement, and fortuitous opinion. I am willing to grant some authority to them, who attribute so little to our prudence; I myself have had some, weak in reason but violent in their persuasion or dissuasion (such promptings were most frequent with Socrates), and I have let myself be carried away by them so fortunately, and so much to my own advantage, that they might have been judged to have something in them of a divine inspiration.
